title: The Limits of a Single Agent — When One Brain Isn't Enough

panels.prompt: A single small figure (representing an AI agent) sits at a massive desk piled impossibly high with papers, documents, and scrolling code printouts. The desk overflows in every direction: code files, test results, error logs, database schemas, API specs, deployment configs cascade off the edges. The figure's eyes are spinning with overwhelm, papers literally falling like an avalanche. Some documents float away. The atmosphere is chaotic but sympathetic -- we feel for this lone worker drowning in complexity. Warm amber desk lamp barely visible under the paper mountain. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, violet (#9F7AEA) glow on the falling papers, warm amber on the lamp

A small cute round ceramic robot with a matte lavender glaze finish, big sympathetic dark-blue eyes, tiny arms crossed thoughtfully, wearing a miniature hard hat, standing next to a towering half-built model skyscraper made of code blocks that is starting to lean dangerously. The robot looks at the overwhelmed desk scene with empathy and understanding. A white speech bubble with black outline near the top. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Even the smartest person can't build a skyscraper alone." Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, soft violet ambient lighting
panels.bubble_text: Even the smartest person can't build a skyscraper alone.
panels.speaker: CERAMIC

panels.text: By late 2024, AI coding agents were genuinely useful. Developers relied on them daily. But a pattern emerged: the harder the task, the more likely the agent was to struggle. Not because the model wasn't smart enough — but because of structural limits that no amount of intelligence could overcome.

panels.text: Vibe Coding: A Cautionary Note. By early 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined the term “vibe coding” — describing what you want in natural language, barely reading the generated code. It captured both the promise and a real peril: what happens when humans stop understanding their own code? Over-reliance on agents risks systems built by AI that no human fully comprehends.

panels.prompt: A visual timeline showing the compounding error problem. Starting from the left with a small red dot labeled 'Minute 5: Slight wrong design choice', the dot sends out ripples that grow into yellow expanding circles labeled 'Minute 15: All code builds on it', then into large orange warning zones labeled 'Minute 30: Tests fail at line 247, not line 5', and finally into a chaotic red explosion labeled 'Minute 45: Agent patches wrong line, more errors'. A dotted line from the chaos points back to the original small red dot with text: 'The root cause is buried.' Dark background with the timeline moving left to right, each stage getting more visually chaotic. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text: A single agent, no matter how capable, is trying to hold an entire project in one context, work on it sequentially, and maintain perfect recall across thousands of steps. That is not how humans build complex things either. Humans build complex things with teams.

“Think about the hardest project you have ever worked on. Could one person have done it alone, no matter how talented? Or did it require different people with different skills, working in parallel, reviewing each other’s work? Now think about why that same logic applies to AI.”

A white speech bubble with black outline above. Inside the bubble the text reads: "One agent is limited. But what about a team?"
